en: When I recall the old days,
These ribs of mine
Part layer from layer.
After that, I went about
Wishing to die and leave this world.
Then I saw your orphaned eyes,
Young falcon left by the hero,
And longed to behold you.
Eager to see you, I hurried,
Staggering beneath firewood,
Beaten with clubs by the herdsmen,
Ravaged and thrashed,
With cudgels raining on my back.
“Master, show me mercy,” I begged,
Pleading even with lowly slaves.
Your uncle went about flayed raw,
With no strength left to fight,
His shoulders deeply gouged.
Your uncle, once like a mighty stallion,
Became pliant as leather,
And all I saw was turmoil.
Instead of food, I drank
Nine bucketfuls of water,
Stretched out like a hide,
While a horse’s knobby ankle bone
Was given me in place of food.
Your uncle suffered pillage,
His precious body endured beatings.
Clubs struck my back,
Spikes pierced my rump.
I set out to gather firewood,
And three times every day
I was wrapped in thorns.
I was mauled by strongmen,
Beaten by the herdsmen.
Long did I carry firewood,
Hoping, if I did not die, to see
The orphan left as our legacy.
May God never inflict upon another
The humiliations I endured,
My son, nor the torment that befell me.
My horns broken, left forlorn,
I came back shorn of all power.
No mortal can deny it.
His fortunes were perfectly balanced;
When you looked into his heart,
It was broader than the whole earth.
God will never create another man
Made like your father.
Your father was a fierce gray-maned lion,
Who tethered fourteen steeds,
And dwelt in central Keng-Kol.
If an enemy came out shooting,
He drove them before him.
Whoever stirred his wrath,
He crushed between his fangs.
My son, such is my story.
Your dear father’s confidant,
The noble Choro, his companion,
Whose stallion carried him to Altai,
Was your father’s kinsman.
They kicked together like foals,
And contended for the same breast.
Liver and choice cuts
Were divided equally for them,
And the countless Nogai and Kyrgyz
Called them the foremost of sons.
So that we might become true brothers,
Our mother Kanykei gave both of us
Milk from her own breast.
From the left breast Kanchoro sucked,
Dark crimson blood flowed.
From the right breast Külchoro sucked,
Pure white milk welled like a spring.
“I have seen an omen in the boys,”
Your sorrowful mother wept.
“Külchoro, for whom milk sprang forth”—
These were my mother Kanykei’s words—
“If Külchoro survives
And you heed my words from the start,
He will be your inheritance and support.
But this Kanchoro here,
To tell you the truth,
Is a cursed and grievous menace;
It shows in your blood-uncle.”
The Jediger surged in wildly,
And mighty Kyyaz emerged as their chief.
The enemy among us was Kanchoro,
Who became a man of infamous name.
He shattered my happiness
And destroyed my golden throne.
He left my people wailing
And broke my back.
He felled my flourishing tree,
And tore down all my dwellings.
He made widows of braided women,
And trampled proud young lords
Underfoot like loose wool.
He bloodied the mouth of my gateway
And turned my black road to dust.
Many powerful lionhearted warriors
He utterly swept away.
At Talas he slaughtered
My giant, Semetey.
He battered my head again and again,
And brought me endless grief.
My helpless people were plundered;
I do not know whether he lives or is dead—
My uncle, heroic Bakai.
He left my land of Talas desolate
And scattered my Kyrgyz people.
He ignored all my pleas
And cut down my remaining men with swords.
In his day your Külchoro
Conquered Beijing and grew mighty,
But parted from his hero,
Your hapless uncle fell into disgrace.
Your father, the formidable Semetey,
Was a lion favored by the spirits.
God will not soon create
Among mortal men
Another like your father.
He was a mighty, steadfast stronghold.
He enslaved in Talas
My mother, noble Kanykei.
The accursed man seized as plunder
My sister-in-law Chachykei.
He drove away and seized my livestock
And drained my blood till I wasted away.
He made me taste bitter salt
And let my daughter be despoiled.
Those witless dogs grew insolent
And turned savagely upon their master.
The strutting villains gathered
And raided my caravan from Keng-Kol.
Grieving and sorely disgraced,
I returned without taking revenge.
They plundered my old people.
Against those swaggering dogs,
Because I stood alone,
I returned unable to ease my pain.
To gird my waist firmly,
To avenge my heroic lord and brother—
My tongue speaks, but I have no strength;
Though I glare at them, I am helpless.
To clash with them and raise a battle,
I no longer have the thick wrists,
The stony heart, or the days I once had.
My two hands can no longer move;
My six limbs are no longer whole.
I no longer have blood surging beneath my skin,
Nor strength to spur against
Those dogs accursed by Heaven.
The thoroughbred once pranced among the herd,
But your uncle’s former valor has departed.
Unable to die though wishing for death,
I languish here like this.
The bright flowers have vanished from the pasture;
Your uncle, once a lion of the world,
Now languishes like this.
If I fought them as an equal,
I no longer have my towering stature.
If I met them face-to-face in battle—
“He will become your enemy,”
My mother had told me.
“That Choro who will turn foe—
Remove him from your sight.
My precious mother Kanykei
Said to cut off his head with a sword.
“His mischief will harm many;
Finish him once and for all.
Set matters right and end our grief;
Let the sorrow people speak of disappear.”
But my foolish uncle, the hopeless man,
Would not hear of it.
“If this lone boy proves a kinsman,
What blessings might he not bring?
And if this boy proves an enemy,
What evil might he do?
If I grow angry, he will die.”
When this boy fixed his hostile gaze
Upon my foster father Chubak,
Upon the young falcon Chubak left behind,
My heedless, misguided uncle
Still would not listen.
He steeped poison in my cup;
Kanchoro brought me to ruin.
He slaughtered and ate the fostered foal,
Yet whenever enemies surrounded us,
He claimed he would be a true brother.
In the end, Kanchoro
Drank spirits and ran mad;
Greedy for blood, he slaughtered my brother.
He drank kumis and ran mad,
And struck down my people in his frenzy.
No pleading moved him;
Though I begged, he would not spare my life.
No entreaty moved him.
He drove away my livestock,
Made my blood flow like water,
And utterly destroyed my honor.
He gave my banner up as spoil
And hacked down my pride with an axe.
If I slaughter one of them, let me
Suck down and swallow his blood.
May I die if I take no vengeance;
If I do not fight to the death for revenge,
May I sink away as though never born.
These two have grown powerful—
Let me test them in furious combat.
Let me grapple and bring destruction,
And take vengeance far and wide.
If death is due, let us die;
Let us meet in combat.
If I do not make this year’s slaughter glorious,
Now that they have fallen within my reach
And the snarling Jediger
Have revealed their enmity;
If I do not thresh them like grain
And bring black disaster
Upon Kyyaz, son of Bagysh;
May I not live, but die.
Mighty Kyyaz is my chosen foe;
Let me try my strength against him.
Standing face-to-face across the field,
Swinging battle-axes and thrusting spears,
Let us fight in a bloody clash.
Gripping the lunging spear,
Let us brace and drive it home,
Lean toward the saddle-girth,
And soak our spears in blood.
If I do not split his head without mercy,
Driving the spear firmly into him—
Its shaft is stout and its point sharp,
The great, deep-grooved war spear—
If we do not thus steep it in blood,
Until the people cry out in turmoil,
Saying, “The champions are at war,”
Until every witness is shaken,
And made to flee;
Until every person who sees it
Despairs of life itself.
A hero should take up his spear,
But my two hands have no vigor.
My strength is spent; I have no power.
Though they still seem to move,
I have scarcely a spoonful of blood.
My heart is flame, my liver embers,
Yet against fiery hero Kyyaz
I have no strength to fight.
Now that I have seen you in this world,
My heart is content with the Creator.”
When Külchoro spoke these words,
Seytek’s heart was overwhelmed.
As he watched,
Tears poured from his eyes.
